abstract: The world is experiencing unprecedented rates of biodiversity loss. To reverse this trend, signatories to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) have committed to conserving at least 30% of marine and terrestrial areas by 2030, with an emphasis on sites critical for biodiversity. One mechanism to support this goal is the identification of Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) to inform spatial planning and the development of conservation area networks. However, few case studies demonstrate how the KBA process can be implemented in high-biodiversity, low-income countries. We present a national-scale example from Mozambique, where KBAs were delineated across seven taxonomic groups, and outline a post hoc theory of change to support broader national implementation and progress towards CBD targets. We describe how the project established institutional arrangements and training to build technical capacity, highlighting the central role of the Ministry of Land and Environment. We then present the KBA identification process and results, including species Red List assessments that contributed to the identification of four marine and 25 terrestrial KBAs. With results integrated into national policy and legislation, the Mozambique KBA system demonstrates that KBA identification is feasible in lower-income countries and provides a model for broader application.
